content.title: About
content.content: Atole de chocolate is a traditional Mexican hot beverage made from corn masa, milk, sugar and cocoa. The drink has a thick, creamy texture and a rich chocolate flavor, often spiced with cinnamon or vanilla.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Atole dates back to pre‑Columbian Mexico, where it was prepared with maize and cacao.
It is traditionally served in clay mugs (cazuelas) to retain heat.
There are many regional variations: some add nuts, others use aromatics like anise or clove.
Atole is commonly served during holidays, especially Day of the Dead and Christmas.
The corn masa used in atole provides complex carbohydrates that release energy slowly.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Corn masa and sugar give a quick boost of energy, useful in cold weather.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa contains flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Corn fiber promotes healthy digestion and gut microbiota.

items.title: Contains calcium and magnesium
items.content: Milk and corn masa supply calcium and magnesium, important for bones and muscles.

items.title: Warm‑soothing effect
items.content: A hot drink helps warm the body and can have a calming effect on the nervous system.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: High sugar levels may be problematic for people with diabetes or weight concerns.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Those with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy should use plant‑based milks.

items.title: Corn cross‑contamination
items.content: While corn is gluten‑free, some masa mixes can be contaminated with gluten, which matters for celiac disease.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The thick beverage is relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve Atole de chocolate hot, typically in 200–250 ml cups. Add a pinch of cinnamon, vanilla, or a piece of chocolate for extra flavor. A dairy‑free version can be made with almond, oat, or other plant milks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry ingredients (masa, cocoa, sugar) in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Prepared atole is best consumed within 2–3 hours; leftovers can be refrigerated and reheated, though the texture may change.

carrots-fresh-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Carrots, fresh, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Carrots are a root vegetable rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A. When boiled without added fat they retain most nutrients, stay sweet and tender, and work well as a side dish or in soups and stews.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Carrots were first domesticated in Central Asia over 5,000 years ago.
The orange color became common in the 17th century after Dutch breeders selected for it.
Raw carrot sticks are often used as a natural “toothpick” for cleaning teeth.
Carrots come in many colors: purple, yellow, white and red as well as orange.
In Japan carrots are frequently cut into thin match‑stick strips (julienne).

items.title: Rich source of beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene is converted to vitamin A, supporting vision, immunity and skin health.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium and antioxidants help regulate blood pressure and reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A 100‑g serving of boiled carrots contains about 35 kcal, making it a weight‑friendly option.

items.title: Contains vitamins K and C
items.content: Vitamin K is important for blood clotting, while vitamin C boosts immunity and iron absorption.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to carrots, such as itching or swelling.

items.title: Excessive beta‑carotene intake
items.content: Very large amounts of carrots can cause carotenemia – a harmless yellowish skin tint that fades after intake is reduced.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: When buying non‑organic carrots, rinse them thoroughly to remove possible chemical residues.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boiled carrots without added fat can be served as a side dish, added to vegetable stews, soups, salads or pureed. They are also easy to dice or cut into sticks for quick preparation.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh carrots in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, preferably in a perforated bag. Keep boiled carrots in an airtight container for 3–4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Garlic bread with melted cheese is a ready‑to‑bake frozen loaf topped with a buttery garlic‑herb spread and shredded cheese. When baked, it develops a crisp crust and a gooey cheese layer.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Frozen bread stays fresh and aromatic for up to 12 months when stored properly.
The garlic‑cheese combination is a staple of Mediterranean cuisine and is often served as an appetizer.
Traditional recipes use Parmesan or mozzarella, but other cheeses can be used as well.
Garlic bread is commonly paired with pasta, soups, and salads.
Quick preparation: only 8‑12 minutes in a preheated oven.

items.title: Rich in garlic compounds
items.content: Garlic contains sulfur compounds that have antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The cheese topping provides calcium, essential for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Cheese adds both dairy and plant‑based protein, contributing to satiety.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The bread supplies quick‑acting carbohydrates useful for replenishing energy after activity.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Bread and cheese contain B1, B2, and B6 vitamins that support metabolism.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or dairy protein allergy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Added salt and cheese increase sodium levels, so people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The combination of bread, butter, and cheese makes the product energy‑dense; moderation is key for weight management.

items.title: Potential trans fats
items.content: Some commercial versions may contain partially hydrogenated oils; choose products labeled trans‑fat free.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bake the frozen loaf in a preheated oven at 200 °C for 8‑12 minutes until golden and bubbly. Serve hot as a snack or alongside pasta, salads, or soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen bread in its original packaging in the freezer at –18 °C. After thawing, consume within 2‑3 days and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator.

content.title: About
content.content: Italian sausage is a traditional pork sausage seasoned with fennel, garlic, paprika and other spices. It is widely used in Italian cuisine, especially in tomato‑based sauces, pasta dishes and pizza.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: There are two main varieties: sweet (with sweet fennel) and hot (with added red pepper).
Traditionally the sausage is made from a blend of pork and beef, though some regions use only pork.
Fennel, the key flavoring, gives the sausage its distinctive anise‑like aroma.
Italian sausage is a staple in dishes like cavatelli with sausage and tomato sauce.
In the United States it is often sold as fresh ground sausage that must be cooked before eating.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Pork provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: The sausage supplies heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains B12, B6 and niacin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: A modest amount of monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats can support heart health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Antioxidants from spices
items.content: Fennel, garlic and paprika provide antioxidant compounds that may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Sausage is often salty; excess sodium can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Saturated fat content may contribute to elevated cholesterol if eaten frequently.

items.title: Allergy to spices
items.content: Some individuals may react to fennel, garlic or other seasonings.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Raw or undercooked sausage can harbor pathogenic bacteria; it should be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 71 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sausage can be pan‑fried, baked, simmered in sauces, added to pasta, pizza, stews or used as a filling for stuffed vegetables and sandwiches. For a lighter dish, trim excess fat before cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh sausage refrigerated at 0–4 °C for 2–3 days. Frozen sausage can be stored up to 2 months at –18 °C. Before use, check for off‑odors or discoloration; discard if any signs of spoilage are present.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken liver is an internal organ of the bird, rich in nutrients. It has a soft texture, a slightly bitter taste, and is commonly used in dishes across many world cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken liver is one of the cheapest sources of high‑quality protein.
In many traditional cuisines it is prepared as pâtés, fried pieces, or added to soups.
The liver accumulates vitamins and minerals, giving it a higher nutritional value than most muscle meats.
Its iron content exceeds that of beef liver.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, immunity, and skin health.

items.title: High iron content
items.content: Iron is essential for hemoglobin formation and preventing anemia.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Liver contains B12, B2, B6, which are involved in energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is important for DNA synthesis and especially beneficial during pregnancy.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Liver protein is highly digestible and supports tissue growth and repair.

items.title: High vitamin A levels
items.content: Excessive intake can cause hypervitaminosis A, particularly in children and pregnant women.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: The liver can accumulate toxins and heavy metals, so choose products from reputable sources.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to liver.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Liver contains a notable amount of cholesterol, so people with hypercholesterolemia should limit consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken liver can be sautéed, stewed, baked, or made into pâté. Before cooking, rinse it, remove any visible vessels, and cut into bite‑size pieces. It pairs well with onion, garlic, apples, and various spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh chicken liver in the refrigerator at 0–2 °C in an airtight container for no more than 1–2 days. For longer storage, freeze it at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 3 months. Before use, check the smell—any sour or off odor indicates spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed potatoes with tomatoes is a dish made from selected potatoes, ripe tomatoes, onion and aromatic spices. The potatoes are simmered until tender, then tomatoes are added to create a rich sauce. The dish is popular in Eastern European and Mediterranean cuisines, often served as a side or a light main course.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stewed potatoes retain most of their vitamin C when cooked gently without prolonged boiling.
Tomatoes added to the dish are rich in lycopene – an antioxidant that becomes more bioavailable after heating.
Traditionally the recipe is prepared in earthenware pots, which help preserve flavor and moisture.
In some regions sweet bell pepper or carrots are added for extra color and taste.
The dish is commonly garnished with fresh parsley or dill for a bright finish.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Potatoes provide slowly digestible carbs that supply steady energy and help maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C and potassium
items.content: Together potatoes and tomatoes deliver vitamin C and potassium, supporting immune function and normal blood pressure.

items.title: Lycopene and antioxidants
items.content: Cooked tomatoes increase lycopene availability, which protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The dish is typically prepared with minimal oil, making it suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Potato skins and tomatoes provide fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes, ranging from skin rashes to gastrointestinal symptoms.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Adding excessive salt can make the dish unsuitable for people with hypertension.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Tomatoes contain oxalates, which in large amounts may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve stewed potatoes with tomatoes hot as a standalone dish or as a side to meat, fish, or legumes. Garnish with fresh herbs, drizzle a little olive oil, or sprinkle with grated cheese for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the dish to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When reheating, add a splash of water or broth to restore moisture.

content.title: About
content.content: Berry strudel is a pastry made from thin rolled dough filled with fresh berries (commonly blueberries, strawberries or a mixed berry blend) and lightly sweetened. The dough is crisp, while the filling is juicy and aromatic. Strudel is often served warm, dusted with powdered sugar.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The traditional Austrian strudel originated in Tyrol in the 19th century.
Berry versions became popular across Europe after frozen berries became widely available in the early 20th century.
The thin dough is made from flour, water, butter and a small amount of eggs, without yeast.
The original recipe used only apples, but berry variations are now considered classic.
Strudel is frequently served with vanilla sauce or ice cream.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Berries provide vitamin C, vitamin E and polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from the berries and whole‑grain dough promotes healthy bowel function.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The dough uses a modest amount of butter, keeping saturated fat levels relatively low.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Flour and eggs supply B1, B2 and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Moderate sugar content
items.content: When prepared with controlled sweetening, the dessert can be a healthier treat.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The dough contains wheat flour, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Overly sweet strudel can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dough and butter make the pastry energy‑dense; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Eggs are commonly used in the dough; they should be substituted for those with an allergy.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve strudel warm, sliced into portions. It can be dusted with powdered sugar, drizzled with melted butter, or accompanied by vanilla sauce, ice cream, or yogurt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep strudel in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Reheat in the oven before serving to restore a crisp crust.
